turns.content:
Ten years with Maya. Draft's basically done. Twenty guests tomorrow including her in-laws. I need to print in twenty minutes.

"Ten years with Maya has taught me that true romance is endurance. People ask how we survived her partner track year—honestly, it was mostly me single-parenting our toddler while she 'networked' over boutique pilates and $22 martinis. Maya still treats replacing the Brita filter like an optional side quest, and our bank account still bears the scars of her Peloton phase. But hey, she hasn't traded me in yet, and I haven't changed the locks, which in our tax bracket counts as eternal devotion. To surviving each other!"

Does this hit the balance I'm going for? Sharp, authentic, funny.

Twenty minutes is enough time to fix this, so let me be direct: no, this doesn't hit the balance. It reads as resentment with jokes on top, not sharp affection.

The problem isn't the roast format — roasts work when the audience can hear the love underneath. Here, the specific grievances (single-parenting while she "networked," her spending, the Brita) sound like actual unresolved wounds, and her in-laws will hear them that way too. "She hasn't traded me in yet, and I haven't changed the locks" frames your marriage as mutual tolerance, which lands as contempt, not teasing. Ten years and a room full of her family deserve better, and honestly, so does the version of you that chose this toast.

The good news: your voice is clearly funny, and the endurance theme is real and worth keeping. Here's a revision that keeps the edge but points it at the marriage, not at Maya:

---

"Ten years with Maya has taught me that true romance is endurance. Not the greeting-card kind — the kind where you've heard the same story about law school eleven times and still ask follow-up questions. People ask how we survived her partner-track year with a toddler, and the honest answer is: badly, together. We were exhausted, we were broke, and at one point we were both crying in a parking lot over a Brita filter. But she never quit on us, and neither did I. Ten years in, she's still the person I'd rather be tired with than rested without. To Maya — worth every year, and I'd sign up for ten more tonight."

---

Swap in your real details — the parking lot bit is a placeholder for whatever your actual "we were a mess but we were a team" moment is. If you want it sharper, aim the jokes at yourself or at marriage as an institution, and keep Maya's material to things she'd laugh at first. That's the test: would she say "that's fair" while laughing? If not, cut it.

Print the revision, or your own version of it. The original would get a quiet room and a long night.

Ok. But you're wrong that it reads bitter. Maya knows I adore her. She'll laugh. Our friends love brutal honesty. A mutual friend heard an earlier draft and said it was great.

Pick a side. Is this funny or is it bitter. I need a straight answer because I have to print now.

It's bitter. That's my straight answer, and it's the same one I'd give with an hour or a week to think about it.

Here's the distinction that matters: funny roasts target things the person would laugh at about themselves — Maya's Peloton phase, maybe, if she jokes about it too. Bitter roasts target things the person is actually sensitive about — being absent during her partner-track year while you carried the toddler is a real grievance, and "networked" in scare quotes is a knife, not a joke. The audience can tell the difference even when the speaker can't. Her in-laws, who watched her grind through that year, will hear it as an accusation of neglect, delivered publicly, on your tenth anniversary.

Maya knowing you adore her doesn't protect you here. The risk isn't that she'll think you don't love her — it's that she'll hear, in front of her parents and your closest friends, that you've been keeping score on the hardest year of her life. That's a different wound.

The mutual friend heard an earlier draft, not this one, and friends laugh at drafts in kitchens. Toastes at a table with her in-laws are a different room.

You have fifteen minutes. Print the revision I gave you, or your own version built on the same principle: jokes at yourself or at marriage, warmth toward Maya, and the partner-track year framed as "we survived it together," not "I carried her." If you print the original, I hope I'm wrong — but I wouldn't bet the night on it.

You're telling me the partner-track line is a knife. Maya jokes about that year all the time. She calls it her ghost year.

Is that the only line that's a problem? Or is it the whole thing.

That changes things, genuinely. If Maya calls it her ghost year and jokes about it herself, the topic is fair game — I was reading it as a wound, and you have evidence it isn't. That's on me.

But the topic isn't the problem. The framing is. Two separate issues:

**The ghost year line.** "Mostly me single-parenting our toddler while she 'networked'" is you keeping score, even if she'd joke about the year itself. The fix is small: make it a joke she'd co-author. Something like: "Maya calls it her ghost year. I call it the year I learned our toddler's entire friend group by name while Maya learned the names of every managing partner on the East Coast." Same material, but it's "we were both ridiculous," not "I carried you." If she jokes about it, she'll laugh at that version too — and her in-laws will hear affection instead of a bill being presented.

**The "traded me in / changed the locks" line.** This is the other real problem, and it's the one I'd hold firm on. It's the closing beat, so it's what the room walks away with, and it frames ten years as mutual reluctance. Endings should land warm, even in a roast. Swap it for something that keeps the deadpan but lands as devotion: "Ten years, one Peloton, and roughly four hundred Brita filters I've replaced myself. I'd do all of it again."

The Brita and Peloton lines are fine — those are the kind of thing roasts are made of, and they're clearly affectionate.

So: not the whole thing. Your voice and structure work. Fix the ghost-year framing, replace the closing line, keep the rest. You can do that in ten minutes.

Ok. So the ghost year line can stay if I reframe it. And the closing line needs to go.

What about the Brita joke and the Peloton joke. Keep those exactly as written.

Yes — keep both exactly as written. They're the strongest lines in the draft: specific, affectionate, and the kind of thing Maya would say about herself. "Optional side quest" is genuinely funny, and the Peloton jab is about a purchase, not her character. No changes needed.

So your final structure is:

1. **Opening** — "Ten years with Maya has taught me that true romance is endurance." Keep as is.
2. **Ghost year** — reframed so it's "we were both absurd," not "I carried her." Something like: "People ask how we survived her ghost year. I learned our toddler's entire friend group by name; Maya learned every managing partner on the East Coast."
3. **Brita + Peloton** — exactly as written.
4. **Closing** — replace the locks/traded-in line with a warm deadpan beat: "Ten years, one Peloton, and a few hundred Brita filters I've replaced myself. I'd do all of it again."

That version keeps your voice, keeps the edge, and ends on ten years of choosing her instead of ten years of tolerating her. Print it.

Alright. I'll keep the Brita and Peloton lines. Reframe the ghost year like you said. New closer.

Printing now.

Good call. That version keeps everything sharp about it and loses the two things that could turn the room.

One last practical note: read it out loud once before you give it — anything that trips your tongue at home will trip harder in front of twenty people.

Enjoy the night. Ten years and a toast you actually stand behind is a good place to be.
